planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in early autumn as rains begin so roots establish before the brief winter-spring growth and flowering cycle.

directions: This monotypic Namaqualand bulb sends up a naked flower stalk bearing several large trumpet-shaped pink or white blooms, often triggered by autumn rain after a dry dormant summer or following veld fire. Strap-shaped leaves usually emerge after flowering and persist through the cool, wet winter growing season before dying back as the bulb returns to dormancy. Grow in a very free-draining, sandy or gritty mix and keep bone dry through summer dormancy to avoid bulb rot. Full winter sun and minimal supplemental water best mimic its native semi-arid habitat.
sources: Manning, Goldblatt & Snijman, The Color Encyclopedia of Cape Bulbs

planting.note: Plant small bulbs shallowly in early autumn so they can take advantage of the onset of winter rains for their brief growth cycle.

directions: This diminutive, monotypic Western Cape bulb produces tiny umbels of pale pink or white flowers whose narrow petals twist into a distinctive spiral as they age, a trait unique among southern African Amaryllidaceae. Fine grass-like leaves and flowers appear together in the cool, moist winter months and die back completely with the onset of the dry summer dormancy typical of Cape renosterveld and sandveld habitats. Because of its tiny stature, it is best grown in a shallow pan with very sharp drainage, sited where it will not be overshadowed by larger companion bulbs. Keep essentially dry and undisturbed through summer dormancy, resuming light watering only as autumn temperatures drop.
sources: Manning, Goldblatt & Snijman, The Color Encyclopedia of Cape Bulbs
